title: The Goodwill Gap: The End-of-Year Spending Most Cash Flow Forecasts Miss
linkedin:
Christmas stock. Extended wage bills. Most cash flow forecasts for the last quarter of the year get those two right.

What quietly misses the forecast is the second wave landing in the exact same six weeks: the staff Christmas function, end of year bonuses, client gifts and hampers. Individually small. Added together, often enough to tip a forecast that was otherwise sound.

None of this is a planning failure. A monthly budget is built for recurring, predictable costs, and goodwill spending is neither. Venue deposits get agreed in a quick conversation, bonus figures get floated months before they are paid, gift lists get built department by department. No single decision feels big enough to earn its own line, so none of them do, until the invoices land together in December.

The fix is not a new process. It is folding this spending into the same weekly forecast that is already tracking stock and wages, while there is still room to make a considered call: bring the function forward a week, stagger a bonus across two pay runs, or simply confirm the number was right in the first place.

September is the window where that is still a decision. December is where it becomes damage control.

For owner-led businesses across Brisbane, Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria, the last quarter of the year usually gets planned around the obvious costs: Christmas stock, casual staffing, and the wage bill for longer trading hours. Those numbers tend to be sized well because most businesses have been through this ramp before.

What often gets missed is a second wave of spending landing in exactly the same few weeks: the staff Christmas function, end of year bonuses, and the client gifts and hampers that keep relationships warm. None of these decisions look large on their own, which is exactly why they rarely earn a line in the cash flow forecast. A venue deposit here, a bonus figure floated in a meeting, a gift list built department by department. By the time December arrives, all of it lands in the same account in the same fortnight as the trading costs already stretching it.

None of this spending is a mistake. The people and clients on the receiving end of it are worth the goodwill. The real risk is only ever the surprise of it arriving unplanned, at the exact point in the year when there is no longer room to move it.

September is still a window to size this properly and fold it into the existing forecast, rather than discover it as December closes in. Read the full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.
